newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan surplus may cloud dollar long-term outlook.
newsitem.headline: Japan surplus may cloud dollar long-term outlook.

text.p: Signs that Japan's trade surplus is again on the rise, which prompted some wary comments by U.S. officials, may cloud longer-term prospects for the dollar's bull run, analysts and dealers said on Thursday.

"A rise in Japan's surplus is not an imminent threat to the dollar but may help produce a fall of five to 10 yen at a time when the dollar's rally is seen as overdone," said Taisuke Tanaka, strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.

Tokyo's surplus in its current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, surged to 150.7 billion yen ($1.24 billion) in January, compared with a surplus of 32.6 billion yen ($269 million) a year earlier, exceeding economists' expectations.
U.S. officials have been voicing concerns that the Japanese trade surplus -- on a declining trend for the past year and a half-- is again on the way up.

When asked about the U.S. trade gap with Japan, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Wednesday, "The broader question is what the Japanese economy will do. I think there is an attitude on our part of being very watchful."

Speaking to reporters after the January surplus was released, Lawrence Greenwood, economic minister-counselor at the U.S. Embassy here, said that Japan needs to take steps to avoid a resurgence in the current account surplus.
But currency dealers said that despite hints of renewed U.S.-Japan tensions over trade, dollar buying by Japanese investors was still the key factor driving dollar/yen trade.
"The important thing now is that there is a constant capital outflow from Japan, even if Japan has a surplus." CSFB's Tanaka said.
But he cautioned that the situation has apparently changed from the past year, when dollar-buying factors dominated.
The dollar was at 121.55 yen in late Tokyo on Thursday, up from 121.25 yen in late New York trade on Wednesday.
A boost in exports, particularly autos, was a key factor in the trade surplus increase, analysts said.
The dollar may come under pressure if Japanese firms rush to export as domestic demand falters because of scheduled tax hikes, they said.
"Each carmaker probably will turn to boost exports temporarily to make up possible dents in demand at home in the April-June period," said a major car industry source.
Japanese car exports to the United States rose 75 percent in January from a year ago and overall vehicle exports posted a 34 percent growth to nearly 355,200 units during the month.
A rise in exports from Japan would mean more downward pressure on the dollar as exporters need to repatriate overseas earnings into yen, analysts said.
